gloss: The basic unit of money in the United States and several other countries.
examples: I found a *dollar* in the parking lot.
He makes about ninety thousand *dollars* a year.
The *dollar* gained against the euro this week.

gloss: A unit of money worth one hundredth of a dollar.
examples: I don't have a *cent* on me.
Every *cent* goes to the animal shelter.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *sent* and *scent* in American English.

gloss: A flat piece of metal used as money.
examples: She dropped a *coin* in the fountain.
He keeps his *coins* in a jar by the door.

gloss: A piece of paper money, or a statement of what you owe.
examples: The electric *bill* was huge this month.
contrast: In the paper-money sense Americans say *bill*; the British say *note*.

gloss: The system of money used in a particular country.
The money returned to you after paying, or coins of small value.
examples: Do you have *change* for a twenty?
I emptied the *change* out of my pockets.
contrast: In the money sense it is uncountable — never *changes*.

gloss: An American coin worth five cents.
examples: He handed me a *nickel* and two dimes.
I found a *nickel* under the couch cushion.

gloss: An American coin worth ten cents.
examples: A phone call cost a *dime* back then.
She counted out four *dimes* for the meter.
I've got a couple of *dimes* in my pocket.

gloss: An American coin worth twenty-five cents, or a three-month business period.
examples: Sales were up in the third *quarter*.
Do you have a *quarter* for the parking meter?
contrast: Two everyday senses: the 25-cent coin and a three-month period of a business year.

gloss: An informal word for a dollar.
examples: He's just trying to make a few extra *bucks*.

gloss: A small folding case for carrying money and cards.
examples: I left my *wallet* in the car.
Somebody lifted his *wallet* on the subway.
Both *wallets* turned up at the lost and found.

gloss: A business that keeps people's money and lends it out.
examples: Most *banks* charge a fee for that.

gloss: An arrangement that lets you keep money at a bank.
examples: I opened a checking *account* last week.
They froze both *accounts* during the investigation.

gloss: Money put into an account, or money left as security.
examples: I made a *deposit* at the ATM.

gloss: An act of taking money out of a bank account.
examples: The *withdrawal* showed up on my statement.
She made a large *withdrawal* on Friday afternoon.

gloss: The amount of money in an account, or the amount still owed.
examples: My account *balance* is down to forty dollars.
They pay off their credit card *balances* every month.

gloss: A movement of money from one account to another.
examples: The wire *transfer* takes two business days.
I set up an automatic *transfer* to savings.
contrast: Noun stress falls on the first syllable (TRANS-fer); the verb stresses the second (trans-FER).

gloss: A bank employee who handles customers' cash at a counter.
examples: Ask a *teller* to order the cash for you.

gloss: A machine that lets you take cash out of your bank account.
examples: Most *ATMs* charge a fee if you're out of network.

gloss: A printed form ordering your bank to pay someone from your account.
examples: He wrote me a *check* for the deposit.
contrast: American spelling is *check*; British English writes *cheque* for the bank sense.

gloss: A record from a bank listing the activity on an account.
examples: My bank *statement* came in the mail.

gloss: Money paid for the use of borrowed money, or earned on savings.
examples: You'll pay a lot of *interest* over thirty years.
contrast: In the money sense it is uncountable — never *interests*.

gloss: A single act of paying, receiving or moving money.
examples: You get ten free *transactions* a month.
Every *transaction* shows up in the app right away.

gloss: An amount of money paid, or the act of paying it.
examples: The first *payment* is due on the first of the month.
He set up automatic *payments* for the utilities.

gloss: A printed proof that you paid for something.
examples: Keep the *receipt* in case you return it.
I can't find the *receipt* for the printer.
contrast: The *p* is silent — say rih-SEET.

gloss: A document sent to a customer listing goods or work and the amount owed.
The ability to buy now and pay later, based on trust that you will repay.
examples: They cut off his line of *credit*.

gloss: An amount taken directly out of a bank account.
examples: There are two *debits* I don't recognize.

gloss: A plastic card that lets you buy things with borrowed money.
examples: He pays off his *credit cards* every month.
They don't take that *credit card* here.

gloss: A number that tells lenders how reliably you repay what you borrow.
examples: A good *credit score* gets you a better rate.
*Credit scores* update about once a month.

gloss: A sum of money borrowed that must be paid back, usually with interest.
examples: They took out a *loan* to fix the roof.
She's still paying off her student *loans*.
The bank approved the *loan* in a week.

gloss: Money that one person or company owes another.
examples: They ran up huge *debts* on credit cards.
contrast: The *b* is silent — it rhymes with *bet*.

gloss: A long-term loan used to buy a house, with the house as security.
examples: Their *mortgage* payment eats half their income.
*Mortgages* got a lot more expensive this year.
contrast: The *t* is silent — say MOR-gij, never mort-gage.

gloss: A person or company that lends money.
examples: Shop around before you pick a *lender*.
The *lender* wanted two years of tax returns.

gloss: One of a series of regular payments toward a larger sum.
examples: You can pay in twelve monthly *installments*.
The last *installment* is due in June.
He missed an *installment* and they called him.
contrast: American spelling doubles the l — *installment*; the British write *instalment*.

gloss: Property promised to a lender in case the borrower cannot repay.
examples: He put up his truck as *collateral*.
The bank wants *collateral* for a loan that size.
Without *collateral*, the rate goes way up.

gloss: A person or company that is owed money.
examples: His *creditors* have been calling all week.
The company owes three *creditors* over a million dollars.
A *creditor* can't just take your paycheck.

gloss: A legal state in which someone cannot pay what they owe.
examples: Medical bills are a leading cause of *bankruptcy*.

gloss: A failure to make payments that you are legally required to make.
The original amount of a loan, apart from the interest on it.
examples: Most of the early payments go to interest, not *principal*.
She put an extra hundred a month toward the *principal*.
The *principal* on the loan is still forty thousand.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *principle*, a rule; the money sense is spelled *principal*.

gloss: The part of a price paid up front, with the rest borrowed.
examples: They're saving for a *down payment* on a house.
Bigger *down payments* mean lower monthly costs.

gloss: The percentage charged for borrowing money or paid on savings.
examples: We locked in a low *interest rate*.
The *interest rate* on that card is brutal.

gloss: Money put into something in the hope of earning more.
examples: Real estate turned out to be a smart *investment*.

gloss: Someone who puts money into a business or asset to earn a return.
examples: He was an early *investor* in the company.
The pitch is aimed at small *investors*.

gloss: A share of ownership in a company that can be bought and sold.
examples: He bought the *stock* at twelve dollars a share.

gloss: The system in which company shares are bought and sold.
examples: He lost a lot of money in the *stock market*.

gloss: One of the equal parts a company's ownership is divided into.
examples: I sold half my *shares* in March.
They bought a hundred *shares* on Monday.

gloss: A certificate showing that a government or company has borrowed from you.
examples: Government *bonds* pay less, but they're safe.
The city issued *bonds* to build the stadium.
He put the money into a ten-year *bond*.

gloss: A share of a company's profits paid out to its shareholders.
examples: That stock hasn't paid a *dividend* in years.

gloss: Someone who owns shares in a company.
examples: Every *shareholder* gets a proxy form in the mail.

gloss: Someone who buys and sells for other people in exchange for a fee.
examples: *Brokers* take a cut of every deal.

gloss: The overall activity of buying and selling a particular thing.
examples: There's a strong *market* for used trucks.

gloss: The value of one country's money expressed in another's.
examples: The *exchange rate* is terrible right now.
Check the *exchange rate* before you convert anything.

gloss: Something valuable that a person or company owns.
examples: Their biggest *asset* is the building itself.
They sold off *assets* to cover the debt.

gloss: A debt or obligation that a person or company owes.
examples: That old warehouse is a *liability*, not an asset.
We're reviewing every *liability* on the books.

gloss: Money available to invest in or run a business.
examples: The startup raised *capital* from three funds.
Most of his *capital* is tied up in real estate.
contrast: Financial *capital* is uncountable; a *capital* meaning a city is a different, countable word.

gloss: The value of what you own once the debt on it is subtracted.
examples: We have a lot of *equity* in the house now.
She took a pay cut in exchange for *equity*.

gloss: A pool of money set aside or invested for a particular purpose.
examples: He moved his savings into an index *fund*.
The scholarship *fund* is out of money.
*Funds* like this one charge low fees.
contrast: In the plural, *funds* often just means available money — insufficient *funds*.

gloss: The profit made on money that was invested.
examples: The fund posted a twelve percent *return*.
*Returns* have been flat for two years.
You won't get that kind of *return* without risk.

gloss: The chance that an investment loses money.
examples: He took a big *risk* with that money.
The *risks* are spelled out in the fine print.

gloss: The money left over after costs are subtracted from income.
examples: They sold the house at a *profit*.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *prophet* in American English.

gloss: Money that a business or investor fails to get back.
examples: The company reported *losses* for the third year running.
He wrote the *loss* off on his taxes.

gloss: All the money a business takes in before costs are subtracted.
examples: Most of their *revenue* comes from advertising.
Ticket sales are the museum's main source of *revenue*.

gloss: Money that a person regularly receives from work or investments.
examples: Their combined *income* is about ninety thousand.
Rent takes a third of my *income*.
He has no other source of *income*.
contrast: Uncountable for one person's earnings — say *a lot of income*, not *incomes*.

gloss: Money that has to be spent on something.
The act of using money, or the total amount used.
examples: Holiday *spending* hit a record this year.

gloss: A plan for how much money will be spent on what.
examples: We blew the *budget* on the kitchen.
The city passed its *budget* last night.

gloss: The amount of money needed to buy, make or do something.
examples: The *cost* of living keeps going up.
They covered the *cost* of the repair.

gloss: The amount of money you must pay for something.
examples: He got a good *price* on the car.

gloss: An amount charged for a service or for the right to do something.
examples: Their *fees* are higher than everyone else's.

gloss: An amount of money billed or taken for something.
examples: There's a *charge* on my card I don't recognize.

gloss: Money the government requires people and businesses to pay.
examples: He does his own *taxes* every April.

gloss: An amount subtracted from income before tax is calculated.
examples: You can take a *deduction* for the home office.

gloss: Money paid back to you for something returned or overpaid.
examples: I'm still waiting on my tax *refund*.
contrast: Noun stress falls on the first syllable (REE-fund); the verb stresses the second (ree-FUND).

gloss: A general rise in prices that makes money worth less.
A period when an economy shrinks and jobs disappear.
examples: He lost the house in the last *recession*.

gloss: The amount by which spending exceeds income.
examples: They ran a *deficit* three years in a row.
Trade *deficits* were the big story that year.

gloss: The whole system of money, work and trade in a place.
The management of money, especially on a large scale.
examples: *Finance* isn't as glamorous as people think.
contrast: In the plural, *finances* means a person's or company's money situation.

gloss: A fixed amount of money paid to an employee, usually monthly or yearly.
The payment an employee receives for a period of work.
examples: Two *paychecks* came up short this month.

gloss: An increase in the amount someone is paid for their work.
examples: I asked for a *raise* and got it.
Nobody's had a *raise* in two years.
contrast: Americans get a *raise*; the British get a *rise*.

gloss: A payment based on a percentage of what someone sells.
examples: He made a fat *commission* on that sale.

gloss: Regular money paid to someone after they stop working.
examples: *Pensions* aren't as common as they used to be.

gloss: The period of life after a person stops working for good.
examples: Most of that money is locked up until *retirement*.

gloss: An arrangement in which you pay a company to cover future losses.
contrast: Uncountable — say *I have insurance*, never *an insurance*.

gloss: The amount paid regularly to keep an insurance policy active.
examples: My *premium* went up after the accident.

gloss: A written insurance contract between a company and a customer.
examples: He took out a life insurance *policy*.
Read the *policy* before you sign it.
contrast: Two senses: an insurance contract, and a rule or course of action.

gloss: A formal request to an insurer for money you believe you are owed.
examples: She filed a *claim* after the storm.
*Claims* take about three weeks to process.

gloss: The amount you pay yourself before insurance starts paying.
examples: A higher *deductible* means a lower premium.

gloss: Money paid regularly for the use of a home or other property.
A person who owns property and rents it out to others.
A person who pays rent to live in or use a property.
examples: He's been a good *tenant* for six years.

gloss: A contract that lets someone use property for a set time in return for payment.
An amount taken off the usual price.
contrast: Noun stress falls on the first syllable (DIS-count); the verb usually stresses the second.

gloss: Something bought for much less than it is worth.
examples: Forty bucks for that coat is a *bargain*.
She hunts for *bargains* at estate sales.
It seemed like a *bargain* until it broke.

gloss: A printed or digital slip that gives you money off a purchase.
examples: I had a *coupon* for a free coffee.

gloss: Something bought, or the act of buying it.
A regular payment for ongoing access to a service.
examples: The *subscription* runs about ten dollars a month.

gloss: A statement of what a job is likely to cost.
examples: I got three *estimates* for the roof.
The *estimate* came in way over budget.
contrast: The noun ends in a weak ES-tuh-mut; the verb ends in a full ES-tuh-mayt.

gloss: A very large amount of money.
examples: He made a *fortune* in real estate.

gloss: Money or property received from someone who has died.
examples: She spent her whole *inheritance* on the boat.
He's waiting on an *inheritance* from an aunt.

gloss: The crime of getting money by deceiving people.
examples: The bank flagged the charge as *fraud*.
*Fraud* costs the industry billions a year.

gloss: A dishonest scheme for taking someone's money.
examples: It turned out to be a *scam*.

gloss: An official examination of financial records.
examples: He got hit with a tax *audit*.

gloss: The work of keeping and checking financial records.
A person who has at least a million dollars.
examples: The town has more *millionaires* than you'd think.

gloss: Someone who starts a business and takes on its financial risk.
examples: The city is full of young *entrepreneurs*.
Every *entrepreneur* I know has failed at least once.
contrast: French spelling, English stress — ahn-truh-pruh-NUR, with the accent on the last syllable.

gloss: A person who buys goods and services for personal use.
examples: The law is there to protect the *consumer*.

gloss: A legally binding agreement between two or more parties.
examples: Read the *contract* before you sign it.
contrast: Noun stress falls on the first syllable (KAHN-trakt); the verb stresses the second (kuhn-TRAKT).

gloss: A maker's written promise to repair or replace a faulty product.
examples: Extended *warranties* are usually a bad deal.

gloss: A firm promise that something will happen or be made good.
contrast: The *u* after the g is silent, and the stress lands on the last syllable.

gloss: The joining of two companies into one.
examples: The *merger* fell apart at the last minute.
There have been three *mergers* in the industry this year.

gloss: Money given for a specific purpose that does not have to be paid back.
examples: She won a *grant* to study abroad.

gloss: A young company built to grow fast, usually on investors' money.
examples: She left the bank for a *startup*.

gloss: The rate at which employees leave and are replaced, or the money a business takes in.
examples: High *turnover* costs more than people think.
They cut *turnover* by raising starting pay.
contrast: In American business English *turnover* usually means staff churn; the British use it for sales revenue.

gloss: The state of having very little money.
examples: The program is aimed at reducing *poverty*.

gloss: Money or services given by an employer or the government beyond wages.
An amount of money given regularly for a particular purpose.
examples: There's a travel *allowance* with the job.

gloss: Money or goods given to help a person or organization.
examples: One anonymous *donation* covered the whole thing.

gloss: An organization that raises money to help people in need.
examples: She gives to three *charities* every year.
The *charity* runs almost entirely on volunteers.

gloss: Extra money given to someone for good service.
examples: The *tip* is already included in the total.

gloss: How much something is worth in money.
examples: The house lost *value* after the flood.

gloss: An amount of money.
examples: Huge *sums* went missing from the account.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *some*.

gloss: Money you must pay as a penalty for breaking a rule or law.
examples: *Fines* double if you don't pay in thirty days.
She got a *fine* for the expired registration.
